slides: Welcome back, and now a new topic, charts and tables.
Every quantitative section has one chart or one table, with a few questions about it. Once we know how to read the page, these questions can be quick points.

slides.say: Here's what a chart set looks like on the exam. First comes a chart or a table. After it come four or five questions about it.
at: After it come four or five

slides.say: How much time should we give the set? About five to six minutes. That's a bit more than a minute for each question.
And here's the important part. We start with the chart, not with the questions. We spend a minute, or a minute and a half, just understanding the chart.

slides: Why? Because every question uses the same chart. Once we understand it, every question gets easier.

slides.say: What do these questions test? One skill. Can we understand data, and draw conclusions from it?

slides: The data can come in a table, or in a few kinds of charts.

slides.say: Many students think that any kind of chart can show up. So they feel there's no way to prepare.
That's not true. The exam uses a few very specific types of charts.
We'll go through all of them in the next lessons. A table, points, lines, bars, and a few more.

slides: Once in a few years, a really different chart shows up. But that's very rare.

slides.say: In about ninety-five percent of the sets, the chart is one of the types we learn here.
Now let's go over the page itself, from the top. At the top there's one line of instructions.
It says, study the chart below, then answer the questions that follow.
So really, there are no special instructions. We read the chart, and we answer the questions.
Under it there's a short explanation. It tells us what the chart describes.
at: It tells us what the chart describes

slides.say: For example, the chart describes the vehicles sold in the years two thousand ten to two thousand thirteen.
At the end of the explanation there's almost always an example.
Sometimes there's no example, but that's rare. And when there is one, it's the most important line on the page.
Why is the example so important? Because it lets us check ourselves.

slides: We read the example. Then we find the same thing in the chart. If we see exactly what the example says, we understand the chart.

slides.say: Let's try it on this bar chart. The example says, in two thousand ten, sixty thousand vehicles were sold.
So we go to two thousand ten, at the bottom. We go up to the top of its bar, and across to the axis. We get to sixty.
at: We go up to the top

slides.say: And the axis says thousands, at the top. So sixty means sixty thousand.
It matches the example, so we understand the chart.
Let's check one more sentence, of our own. In two thousand thirteen, a hundred thousand vehicles were sold.
We go to two thousand thirteen, up to its bar, and across. We get to a hundred, so a hundred thousand. It matches again.
at: up to its bar, and across

slides: And if it didn't match? Then our reading is wrong somewhere. Maybe we read the wrong axis, or we missed the units. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next part.
